title: Tria capita ex opere quodam majori inedito de theoria lunae

deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler is computing the Moon's apparent diameter and horizontal parallax for eclipse calculations. Both are proportional to c/z, where z is the true Earth–Moon distance and c its mean value. On the previous page he wrote z/c as a trigonometric series in v (the Moon's eccentric anomaly), V (the Sun's anomaly) and η (the elongation). He then inverted it term by term, using 1/(1+x) = 1 − x + x² − x³, keeping products to second order. This page has three parts.

(1) Numerical inversion. The page gives the finished series
c/z = 1.00160 − 0.05464 cos v + 0.00148 cos 2v + 0.00012 cos V − 0.00018 cos(v+V) + 0.00018 cos(v−V) − 0.00029 cos η + 0.00752 cos 2η + 0.00076 cos(2η−2v) − 0.01061 cos(2η−v) − 0.00020 cos(2η+V) − 0.00025 cos(2η−V) + 0.00019 cos(2η−v+V) + 0.00012 cos(2η−v−V).
Log10 values (characteristic +10) are printed beneath each coefficient.

(2) Scaling to angles. Each coefficient is multiplied by the mean diameter and the mean parallax. The printed logarithms show the multipliers actually used:
- diameter: log 3.27265 ≈ 1873.5″ = 31′13½″, the value of the previous page (the marginal note had proposed 31′14½″);
- parallax: log ≈ 3.53128 ≈ 3398.5″, i.e. essentially 56′39″.
This gives
D = 31′17″ − 102.4″ cos v + 2.8 cos 2v + … + 14.1 cos 2η + 1.4 cos(2η−2v) − 19.9 cos(2η−v) + …
π = 56′44″ − 185.7 cos v + 5.1 cos 2v + … − 1.0 cos η + 25.5 cos 2η + 2.6 cos(2η−2v) − 36.1 cos(2η−v) + …

(3) §7 truncation. Since 1–2″ accuracy suffices, terms below about 1″ are dropped:
D = 31′17″ − 102 cos v + 3 cos 2v + 14 cos 2η + cos(2η−2v) − 20 cos(2η−v)
π = 56′44″ − 186 cos v + 5 cos 2v − cos η + 25 cos 2η + 2 cos(2η−2v) − 36 cos(2η−v)
The cos η term (parallactic inequality, about 1″) survives only in the parallax.

Physically:
- the cos v terms are the elliptic part;
- cos 2η is the variation;
- cos(2η−v) is the evection;
- cos η is the parallactic term.

Euler then remarks that no special tables are needed, because his tables already give the Earth–Moon distance, from which D and π follow easily. He also notes that D is geocentric, and the topocentric (augmented) diameter for any altitude follows readily.

The page serves the next page's §8: in syzygies (conjunction/opposition) and quadratures, η is fixed, and D and π reduce to functions of v alone.

Verification: I recomputed the c/z coefficients from the logarithms of the previous page. The following check:
- cos 2η: e − kg + kh = 0.006978 − 0.000021 + 0.000556 = 0.007513 ✓
- cos(2η−v): h + ke + kf = 0.010607 ✓
- cos(2η−2v): f + kh = 0.000760 ✓
- cos v: k + eh + fh + ¾k³ ≈ 0.05465 ✓
- cos 2v: ½k² = 0.001482 ✓
- cos(v+V): b + ak − jh = 0.000181 ✓

The angular coefficients reproduce from the printed logs (e.g. 7.87564 + 3.27265 = 1.14829 → 14.07″; 8.02571 + 3.53128 = 1.55699 → 36.06″).
errors: Constant term of c/z: Euler's own formula 1 + ½k² + ½h² gives 1.001534 (1.00156 if ½e² is added). Euler prints 1.00160, with log 0.00069, which corresponds to 1.00159. The effect is about 0.1″ in diameter and 0.2″ in parallax, so it is negligible at the stated accuracy.
cos V coefficient: a + kb − kc − hl − hm ≈ 1.40e-4, whereas 1.2e-4 is printed (log 6.07918). This is negligible (≈0.05″).
cos(v−V) coefficient: c − ak + k̃h ≈ 1.86e-4, but Euler gives the identical log 6.25527 as for cos(v+V) (1.80e-4). This looks like a copied value; it is negligible.

Diameter line: the printed log 9.736 for cos η gives 0.545″, so it should round to 0.5, not the printed 0.6. Likewise log 9.679 for cos(2η−V) gives 0.478″, so 0.5 rather than the printed 0.4. Both are rounding or typesetting slips.
Parallax line: log 0.702 gives 5.04″, so 5.0 rather than the printed 5.1.

The diameter is scaled with 31′13½″, although the footnote on the previous page proposes 31′14½″. With that value every diameter coefficient would increase by about 0.05% and the constant would become ≈31′18″.
The mean parallax (≈56′44″) is about 18″ below the modern value (57′02.6″). This reflects the parallax constant of Euler's era and is not a computational error.

ideas.what: Inverting a trigonometric series for z/c into one for c/z by binomial expansion, with products of cosines reduced to sums
ideas.modern_name: Reciprocal of a Fourier series via perturbative (geometric-series) expansion
ideas.where_published: Throughout Euler's lunar theories, e.g. Theoria motus lunae (E418, 1772)

ideas.what: Apparent lunar diameter and horizontal parallax expressed as trigonometric series containing elliptic, variation, evection and parallactic terms
ideas.modern_name: Lunar parallax series (the 'sine parallax' series of later theories)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Mayer's tables, Euler; later Laplace, Brown
ideas.where_published: Euler's lunar tables accompanying E418 give distance/parallax; this explicit diameter series is perhaps only in E838

ideas.what: Truncating the series to the precision needed (1–2″) for eclipse work
ideas.modern_name: Precision-driven truncation of an ephemeris series

ideas.what: Distinction between the geocentric apparent diameter and the diameter seen at a given altitude
ideas.usually_credited_to: Known since early modern astronomy (Kepler et al.)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine numerical page. It converts a distance series into diameter and parallax series by standard series inversion, with only minor arithmetic and rounding slips. It contains no new method or connection; the only interest is as a record of Euler's numerical lunar constants (coefficients ≈102″ and 186″ for the elliptic term, ≈36″ for evection in parallax).
transcription_corrections: The transcription uses ϱ for the eccentric anomaly; on the neighbouring pages it is written v. These are the same variable.
Diameter first line: '102'',4' should read 102″,4 (seconds), as printed.
The printed log under −0,6 cos η in the diameter (9,736) corresponds to 0.5″; the image clearly shows 0,6, so this is an error in the original, not in the transcription.
§7 diameter: the log under 3 cos 2ϱ is printed as 0,444 (image), consistent with the transcription.
